title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Michigan | Genstone
metaDescription: Michigan renovation contractor for investors in Detroit, Grand Rapids, Lansing, Flint and Ann Arbor: pre-offer rehab reviews, permitted work, draw-based pay.
intro: Michigan’s investor housing was largely built by and for the auto industry and the universities, and that history shows up in every rehab we price across the state: brick bungalows and two-family flats in Detroit, worker cottages beside old plant sites in Flint and Lansing, Victorians cut into apartments in Grand Rapids, and student houses within walking distance of campus in Ann Arbor. Nearly all of it predates 1978, sits on a basement in frost-heaving soil and has to get through a long, wet winter every year. Genstone Construction renovates these homes for fix-and-flip investors, BRRRR and buy-and-hold landlords, small multifamily owners, FHA 203(k) buyers and the servicers and GSEs that manage REO. Every project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, moves to an itemized scope with a draw schedule, and runs under one field manager while vetted, licensed Michigan contractors do the work. You pay nothing upfront, and each draw follows completed work.

sections.h2: Michigan housing and what it means for a rehab
sections.body:
Across Michigan’s older cities, the housing that investors buy was mostly built between the 1890s and the 1950s, when manufacturing pulled workers into Detroit, Flint, Lansing and Grand Rapids faster than builders could keep up. The result is a deep stock of frame and brick houses on narrow lots: bungalows, foursquares, colonials, Tudors, gable-front cottages and, in Detroit especially, upper-and-lower two-family flats. After the war came ranches, Cape Cods and split-levels on the edges of each city and in the inner suburbs.

Those eras bring a predictable list of work. Knob-and-tube and cloth-insulated wiring survives behind plaster. Water lines tend to be corroded galvanized steel feeding cast-iron stacks, and the run to the street is usually clay tile that roots found long ago. Old boilers and gravity furnaces may be wrapped in asbestos, and lead paint is a near certainty on windows, porches and trim. Michigan houses almost always have basements, built of fieldstone, brick, block or poured concrete, and many show seepage, efflorescence or frost-driven cracking. The state has also committed water systems to replacing lead service lines over time, but plumbing inside the house remains the owner’s responsibility. A sound Michigan scope prices these items first and the finishes second.

Michigan’s markets behave very differently from one another. In metro Detroit, the brick neighborhoods of the city’s west and east sides support retail flips and FHA 203(k) sales, while large parts of the city and the two-family flats favor long-term rentals and BRRRR, often purchased through the Detroit Land Bank Authority or at auction. REO properties here frequently arrive scrapped or freeze-damaged.

Grand Rapids and West Michigan are tight, competitive markets where owner-occupants outbid investors on clean houses, so opportunities tend to be properties with deferred maintenance, foundation issues or old conversions. Flips work in Eastown, East Hills and Alger Heights, while rentals and BRRRR cluster on the southeast and west sides.

In mid-Michigan, Lansing offers a broad tenant base from state government, hospitals, the plants and the university, and the Eastside and REO Town attract many small investors. Flint has the lowest acquisition prices of the group, but repair costs do not shrink to match, so holds generally outperform flips outside a handful of owner-occupant neighborhoods. Ann Arbor sits at the other end: high prices, intense student rental demand and strict rental certification, where value often comes from adding legal bedrooms rather than cosmetic upgrades.

Michigan builds under statewide construction codes, including the Michigan Residential Code, adopted through the state’s Bureau of Construction Codes within the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, usually called LARA. Most cities, including Detroit, Grand Rapids, Lansing, Flint and Ann Arbor, enforce those codes through their own building departments, and the state handles enforcement in communities that do not. Electrical, plumbing and mechanical work requires permits pulled by appropriately licensed trades, with rough and final inspections.

Contractors who build or remodel homes for others need a residential builder or maintenance and alteration contractor license from LARA, and electricians, plumbers and mechanical contractors carry their own state licenses. Genstone coordinates Michigan contractors who hold the licenses their trades require and who carry insurance.

Local rules layer on top. Detroit requires rental registration, a Certificate of Compliance and lead clearance. Grand Rapids, Lansing and Ann Arbor each run rental certification programs with periodic reinspection, and Ann Arbor’s certificate sets maximum occupancy. Historic district commissions in Detroit, Grand Rapids and Ann Arbor review exterior changes in designated areas. Federal lead-safe work practices apply to almost any rehab that disturbs paint in pre-1978 housing. Our field managers confirm the jurisdiction and requirements for each address before work is priced.

Michigan’s climate drives both scope and schedule. Winters are long and cold, with repeated freeze-thaw cycles that crack concrete steps and driveways, loosen chimney mortar and push against basement walls. On the west side of the state, lake-effect snow off Lake Michigan adds heavy roof loads and ice dams on poorly insulated older homes. Vacant houses are at the greatest risk: when the heat is off, supply lines freeze and split, and an open curb stop can flood a house from the top floor down. Any purchase or REO takeover between late fall and early spring should start with winterization or restoring heat.

Spring is when basements are tested. Snowmelt and heavy rain saturate clay soils, groundwater rises and rivers such as the Grand, the Red Cedar, the Huron and the Flint can flood low areas. Detroit’s combined sewer system can back up into basements during intense summer storms, and many Ann Arbor homes depend on sump pumps installed when the city disconnected footing drains. Summers are warm and humid, feeding mold in damp basements.

Most investors plan interior demolition, rough-ins and finishes for the colder months and schedule roofing, masonry, siding, concrete and exterior paint from late spring through early fall. In student markets, the summer lease turnover adds another hard deadline.

faqs.q: Which Michigan cities does Genstone work in?
faqs.a: Our Michigan city pages cover Detroit, Grand Rapids, Lansing, Flint and Ann Arbor, and we also coordinate licensed contractors in the surrounding suburbs and townships, such as Dearborn, Wyoming, East Lansing, Burton and Ypsilanti. Genstone’s office is in Romeoville, Illinois, and we do not claim local offices in Michigan. Instead, we manage vetted, licensed local trades under a Genstone field manager, which is how we combine national scale with local execution.

faqs.q: What does the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review include for a Michigan property?
faqs.a: You send the address, photos and any inspection notes, and our estimators price the likely repairs, paying close attention to the items that most often break Michigan budgets: scrapped or frozen plumbing, old wiring, wet or bowed basement walls, clay sewer laterals, roofs and lead paint. We then compare the total against the after-repair value or rent your plan assumes and tell you whether the offer still makes sense, before you commit any capital.

faqs.q: Do Michigan contractors need a state license for renovation work?
faqs.a: Yes. Contractors who remodel homes for others generally need a residential builder or maintenance and alteration contractor license from LARA, and electrical, plumbing and mechanical work requires licensed trades who pull permits. Genstone coordinates contractors who hold the licenses their work requires and carry insurance. Using licensed trades keeps permits and inspections straightforward and protects you when a buyer, lender or city inspector asks about the work.

faqs.q: How are draws and payments handled on Michigan projects?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Each project has a draw schedule tied to defined milestones, such as rough-ins passing inspection or drywall complete, and a draw is released only after that work is finished and documented with photos. Dumpster and debris costs are included in the estimate. Lien waivers are collected from the trades as they are paid, and final payment comes after completion and your approval, followed by our one-year workmanship warranty.
